content: Several anticonvulsant medications are utilized in the treatment of neuropathic pain. Oxcarbazepine, a drug closely related to carbamazepine, has been reported to be effective in managing neuropathic pain. However, evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) regarding its efficacy is inconsistent. Oxcarbazepine is considered to have better tolerability compared to carbamazepine. This review is an update of a previous analysis published in 2013. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of oxcarbazepine in treating various types of neuropathic pain. A comprehensive search was conducted on November 21, 2016, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase. Additional searches were performed in the Chinese Biomedical Retrieval System (from January 1978 to November 2016), as well as in the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) databases and the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform in January 2017. The authors also contacted manufacturers of oxcarbazepine and pain experts for supplementary information. The review included all RCTs and randomized cross-over studies that investigated oxcarbazepine for neuropathic pain in individuals of any age or sex. Eligible trials compared oxcarbazepine to placebo or other interventions, with a treatment duration of at least six weeks, regardless of the route of administration or dosage. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were employed for data collection and analysis. Five multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trials involving a total of 862 participants met the inclusion criteria. Three trials focused on painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) (n = 634), one trial examined neuropathic pain due to radiculopathy (n = 145), and one newly identified trial investigated peripheral neuropathic pain of mixed origins, including polyneuropathy, peripheral nerve injury, or postherpetic neuralgia (n = 83). Not all studies reported all outcomes of interest. For painful DPN, one trial reported that 34.8% of participants in the oxcarbazepine group experienced at least a 50% reduction in pain scores after 16 weeks of treatment, compared to 18.2% in the placebo group (risk ratio [RR] 1.91, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.08 to 3.39; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome [NNTB] 6, 95% CI 3 to 41). Similarly, 44.9% of participants in the oxcarbazepine group reported at least a 30% reduction in pain scores, compared to 28.6% in the placebo group (RR 1.57, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.44; NNTB 6, 95% CI 3 to 114; n = 146). These results were derived from a single trial, as two other trials that showed minimal or no benefit did not provide data suitable for meta-analysis. Despite the robust design of these trials, issues such as incomplete outcome data and potential unblinding due to noticeable adverse effects introduced a high risk of bias. Additionally, there was significant imprecision and a high risk of publication bias. In the radiculopathy trial, oxcarbazepine did not demonstrate any benefit for achieving at least 50% pain relief. In the trial involving mixed neuropathies, 19.3% of participants receiving oxcarbazepine achieved at least 50% pain relief, compared to 4.8% in the placebo group. However, these small trials had low event rates and provided, at best, low-quality evidence for any outcome. The proportion of participants reporting improved or very much improved pain was 45.9% in the oxcarbazepine group compared to 30.1% in the placebo group for DPN (RR 1.46, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.88; n = 493; 2 trials; very-low-quality evidence). For radiculopathy, 23.9% of participants in the oxcarbazepine group reported improvement, compared to 14.9% in the placebo group (RR 1.61, 95% CI 0.81 to 3.20; n = 145). No trials were identified for other types of neuropathic pain, such as trigeminal neuralgia. Adverse effects were generally mild to moderate in severity. Based on moderate-quality evidence from the three DPN trials, serious adverse effects occurred in 8.3% of participants receiving oxcarbazepine, compared to 2.5% in the placebo group (RR 3.65, 95% CI 1.45 to 9.20; n = 634). The number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) was 17 (95% CI 11 to 42). In the radiculopathy trial, the RR for serious adverse effects was 3.13 (95% CI 0.65 to 14.98; n = 145). The fifth trial did not provide data on serious adverse effects. More participants discontinued treatment due to adverse effects in the oxcarbazepine group compared to the placebo group. For DPN, 25.6% of participants in the oxcarbazepine group withdrew due to adverse effects, compared to 6.8% in the placebo group (RR 3.83, 95% CI 2.29 to 6.40). For radiculopathy, 42.3% of participants in the oxcarbazepine group withdrew, compared to 14.9% in the placebo group (RR 2.84, 95% CI 1.55 to 5.23). In the mixed neuropathic pain trial, 13.5% of participants in the oxcarbazepine group withdrew, compared to 1.2% in the placebo group (RR 11.51, 95% CI 1.54 to 86.15). In conclusion, this review found limited evidence to support the effectiveness of oxcarbazepine in treating painful diabetic neuropathy, neuropathic pain from radiculopathy, and mixed neuropathies. While some very-low-quality evidence suggests potential efficacy, the small size of the trials, low event rates, heterogeneity in outcome measures, and high risk of publication bias significantly reduce confidence in these findings. Adverse effects, including serious adverse effects and treatment discontinuation due to adverse effects, appear to be more common with oxcarbazepine than with placebo. Further well-designed, multicenter RCTs are needed to investigate the efficacy of oxcarbazepine for various types of neuropathic pain, and selective publication of studies or data should be avoided.
